questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Deduction of a height difference from two echo delays
questions.learningObjective: Explain how two echo delays give a height difference
questions.stem: Explain how two echo delays taken to two points at the same horizontal distance from a radar can be turned into a height difference.

answer.exemplar: Each echo delay gives a total path length by multiplying the delay by the pulse speed, and that path is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose horizontal side is the known offset to the radar. Taking the square root of the path squared minus the offset squared gives the height of each point, and the difference between the two heights is the required height difference, provided the pulse speed and the offset are known accurately.

questions.explanation: Each delay gives a slanted path, and Pythagoras with the known horizontal offset gives each height. Subtracting the heights yields the difference, so the offset and pulse speed must both be known well.
questions.hint: Convert each path to a height before subtracting.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Correction for the mass of the spring itself
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a spring mass correction is applied
questions.stem: A planner needs the period of a spring oscillator but the spring itself has mass. Explain why the effective mass used in the period formula is larger than the mass of the load, and by how much.

answer.exemplar: Only about one third of the spring's own mass moves in step with the load at any instant, because the mass along the spring is distributed along its length and each part has a different amplitude. The standard correction replaces the load mass m by m plus one third of the spring mass, so a light spring barely changes the period while a heavy spring lengthens it appreciably.

questions.explanation: Each part of the spring moves with a different amplitude, so only about a third of the spring's mass adds effectively to the load. The period uses m plus one third of the spring mass.
questions.hint: Think about how much of the spring moves with the load.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Centre of mass of a set of moving masses
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the centre of mass of moving masses is found
questions.stem: A transit planner weighs three loaded pallets moving at different speeds. Explain how to find the centre of mass of the system from their masses and velocities.

answer.exemplar: The centre of mass of a collection of particles is the mass-weighted average of their positions, and for particles that move with constant velocity the position of the centre of mass at any instant follows the same motion as a single body whose mass is the total mass. In practice one computes the total momentum, total mass and the initial positions, then adds the momentum divided by total mass times the elapsed time to the initial centre of mass position.

questions.explanation: Each pallet contributes its mass times its velocity to the total momentum, and the centre of mass moves at the total momentum divided by the total mass. Its starting position is found the same way, weighted by mass.
questions.hint: Weight positions by mass, and use momentum for the motion.

questions.stem: A vibrating floor panel is driven with 60 N at a frequency far from its 4.00 Hz natural frequency. Its steady amplitude is 5.0 mm and its stiffness is 3000 N per metre. What percentage of the static deflection is the steady amplitude?
questions.explanation: The static deflection under the same force is 60 / 3000 = 0.020 m, or 20 mm, and the steady amplitude of 5.0 mm is a quarter of that. Off resonance the response is much smaller than the static value.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Amplitude of a spring oscillator released from rest
questions.learningObjective: Describe how the release point sets the amplitude
questions.stem: Describe how the amplitude of a spring oscillator released from rest is set, and what happens to the motion if the release point is moved further from equilibrium.

answer.exemplar: A mass released from rest starts at a turning point, so the amplitude of the resulting simple harmonic motion is exactly the distance between the release point and the equilibrium position of the spring. If the mass is released further from equilibrium, the amplitude grows in direct proportion to that starting displacement, while the period of the oscillation stays fixed because it depends on the mass and the stiffness rather than on the amplitude.

questions.explanation: Released from rest the mass starts at a turning point, so its distance from equilibrium is the amplitude. Releasing further out increases the amplitude but leaves the period, set by mass and stiffness, unchanged.
questions.hint: A mass at rest starts at a turning point.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Acceleration opposing displacement in simple harmonic motion
questions.learningObjective: Explain the relation between restoring acceleration and displacement
questions.stem: A tram ticket machine's swinging flap returns to rest. Explain how its restoring acceleration is related to its displacement and what that implies about the motion.

answer.exemplar: In simple harmonic motion the acceleration always points back towards the equilibrium position and its size grows in proportion to how far the body has moved away from equilibrium, so a = minus omega squared times the displacement. Because the acceleration is opposite to the displacement and proportional to it, the motion is a pure sinusoid with a single natural frequency, and the restoring force depends on where the body sits rather than on how fast it is moving.

questions.explanation: The acceleration opposes the displacement and grows in proportion to it, the signature of simple harmonic motion. A force depending on speed or on the square of displacement would give a different motion.
questions.hint: Think of a minus sign in front of omega squared.

questions.topic: Conditions on the swing needed for a pendulum to time properly
questions.learningObjective: List the conditions a pendulum needs to keep accurate time
questions.stem: A transit authority is testing a pendulum regulator on a tilting tram. Describe the conditions on the swing under which the pendulum can keep accurate time.

answer.exemplar: The period of a simple pendulum depends very slightly on the amplitude of the swing, so the swing angle must be held small, typically within a few degrees, for the clock to keep true time. The support must also be free to swing without friction or extra restoring force, the length must stay constant, and any change in the amplitude or the supporting acceleration must be corrected before the clock is trusted.

questions.explanation: Accuracy needs a small swing angle, a fixed length, a support that swings freely without friction, and a steady acceleration. Any of these changing makes the true period differ from the regulated value.
questions.hint: Small angle, fixed length, free support, steady acceleration.
